title: The medieval trade of the Black Sea
content: The Black Sea in the medieval centuries carried a trade that joined the steppe, the Mediterranean, and the roads running east across Asia, and the cities along its shores grew rich on traffic that mostly passed through them. Grain moved south, timber and furs came down the rivers, and goods from far inland reached ports where merchants from distant cities kept their own quarters. The record shows towns that were multilingual by need and built around the seasons of the shipping. What made these ports valuable was their place between systems that could not otherwise reach one another. Steppe peoples made goods that Mediterranean cities wanted and wanted goods the steppe could not make, yet neither side travelled the whole way. The ports supplied the middlemen, the warehouses, and the credit that let a cargo be sold several times before it reached a buyer. Their wealth therefore rested on staying useful rather than on making anything. That dependence made them fragile. When the roads across Asia were cut, or when a rival power closed the straits, the traffic fell and the cities shrank quickly. Digging shows them contracting within a generation at several sites, and the medieval papers record merchants moving to wherever the trade had gone. The pattern repeats often enough that historians treat it as typical of towns built on transit rather than on making things.
